e.etymology: A short form of names such as Irene, Serena and Renata that stood on its own by the late 1800s. It is also a spelling of Hebrew Rina, 'joy, song', and a Japanese name written with various kanji.
A modern spelling of Caitlin, the Irish form of Katherine, which came through Old French Cateline. English speakers began saying it KAYT-lin in the 1970s, and dozens of spellings followed.
A less common spelling of Carly, a feminine form of Carl that came into use in the later 20th century and also a pet form of Carla, Carlene and Carlotta. Carl comes from Germanic karl, 'free man'.
The Hebrew original of Elizabeth, from El, 'God', and a root meaning 'to swear an oath'. In Exodus Elisheva is the wife of Aaron, the first high priest.
A modern American name using the -iyah ending of Aaliyah. It also matches Ziya, a form of Arabic Diya, 'light, splendor', which is traditionally a man's name.
From Hebrew ezri, 'my help', from the same root as Ezra. In 1 Chronicles Ezri oversees the farm workers of King David. In the US the name is now given mostly to girls.

assoc.t: Ezri Dax, officer in Star Trek: Deep Space Nine

e.etymology: Spanish and Catalan for 'sea', from Latin mare. As a girl's name it comes from María del Mar, a title of the Virgin Mary as Our Lady of the Sea.
e.note: In English, to mar something means to damage or spoil it.

e.etymology: A respelling of Maisie, a Scottish pet form of Mairead, the Gaelic Margaret, from Greek margarites, 'pearl'. Dr. Seuss used this spelling for the lazy bird in Horton Hatches the Egg.

assoc.t: Mayzie, lazy bird in Dr. Seuss's Horton Hatches the Egg

e.etymology: Coined for Aerith Gainsborough, the flower seller in the 1997 Japanese video game Final Fantasy VII; its makers based the name on the English word earth. Early English versions spelled it Aeris.

assoc.t: Aerith Gainsborough, Final Fantasy VII heroine

e.etymology: A Turkish name from esmer, 'dark, dusky', and ay, 'moon'. American parents also like it as a longer form of Esme.
A modern American coinage joining the Bray- of Brayden and Braylon to the -lynn ending. Braelynn is the more common spelling.
An English spelling of Irish Úna, probably from Old Irish uan, 'lamb'. Oonagh is queen of the fairies in Irish folklore. The name is also popular in Finland.

assoc.t: Oona, mermaid in Nick Jr.'s Bubble Guppies

e.etymology: From Old Norse Ragnarr, from regin, 'counsel' (also 'the gods'), and herr, 'army'; a cousin of German Rainer. The legendary Viking Ragnar Lothbrok, hero of the TV series Vikings, drove its recent US rise.
namesakes: Ragnar Lothbrok (legendary Viking, lead of the TV series Vikings)

assoc.t: Ragnar Lothbrok, Viking hero of the TV series Vikings
Ragnar Relay, overnight team running races

e.etymology: A modern respelling of Jacob, from Hebrew Yaakov. Genesis links the name to the word for heel, because Jacob was born holding the heel of his twin, Esau.
A modern Indian name, generally taken as a feminine counterpart of Krish, the short form of Krishna.

The feminine of the Roman family name Cassius. It is also the name of the cassia tree, whose bark is sold as cinnamon; that word comes through Greek kasia from a Hebrew root shared with the biblical Keziah.

assoc.t: cassia, the cinnamon-like spice and the tree it comes from

e.etymology: A modern name used mostly in Puerto Rican and other Caribbean Latino families, in the pattern of Hebrew-style names ending in -iel such as Ariel and Yadiel.
Best known as the spelling of Aerith used in the first English release of the video game Final Fantasy VII (1997). It also matches Latin aeris, 'of the air'.

assoc.t: Aeris (Aerith) Gainsborough, Final Fantasy VII heroine

e.etymology: From Hebrew raz, 'secret, mystery', and El, 'God'. In Jewish mystical tradition Raziel is the archangel who keeps divine secrets, credited with the Book of Raziel.

assoc.t: Raziel, vampire hero of the Legacy of Kain video games
the angel Raziel in The Mortal Instruments novels

e.etymology: The Yiddish pronunciation of Hebrew Shalom, 'peace', as said in the dialects of Polish and Hungarian Hasidic communities. In the US it is used almost entirely by Hasidic families.
A spelling of Carly, a feminine form of Carl that came into use in the later 20th century and also a pet form of Carla, Carlene and Carlotta. Carl comes from Germanic karl, 'free man'.
The Spanish form of Braulius, the name of a 7th-century bishop and saint of Zaragoza. Its roots are uncertain, possibly Germanic.
From Hebrew: a spelling of Ilan, 'tree', and a variant of the biblical Elon, 'oak tree'. It also matches the English word elan, borrowed from French for spirited energy and style.

assoc.t: elan, the English word for flair and spirited energy

e.etymology: From Arabic minha, 'gift, grant', from the verb manaha, 'to bestow', and understood as a gift from God. It is popular in Pakistan and Bangladesh and with South Asian Muslim families in the US.
A modern American name that blends the sound of Jermaine and Germany with the -ani ending of Armani and Imani.
A form of the biblical Athaliah, usually read as Hebrew for 'the Lord is exalted'. Athaliah was the only woman to rule Judah as queen; Racine and Handel both wrote works about her.
e.note: In the Bible Queen Athaliah takes the throne of Judah by killing the royal heirs.

e.etymology: A modern American coinage that puts a Z in front of Alayah, in the family of Aaliyah, Malayah and Zaliyah.
From Sanskrit vyoman, 'sky, heaven, space'. A modern Indian boy's name.
From the English surname and place name Lynn, from a Celtic word for a lake or pool (Welsh llyn). It also grew out of names ending in -lyn and -line such as Carolyn, and is a favorite middle name.
namesakes: Lynn Swann (Hall of Fame Steelers receiver)
Lynn Anderson (country singer of Rose Garden)

assoc.t: Lynn, Massachusetts, city north of Boston

e.etymology: From the Irish surname Keeley or Keely, an English form of Ó Caollaidhe, from a personal name based on caol, 'slender'.
A modern American name that spells out the initials J.C. or builds on Jay with the ending of Stacie and Kacie. Its 1996 peak came as gymnast Jaycie Phelps won Olympic team gold.
From the name of Germany's capital, which probably goes back to an old Slavic word for a swamp. Berlin is also a German and English surname, as in songwriter Irving Berlin.

assoc.t: Berlin, heist leader in Netflix's Money Heist
Berlin, 1980s band behind Take My Breath Away
